claims.text: Boride-based components in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment are directly exposed to molten aluminum at around 660°C.
Direct exposure to molten aluminum causes rapid surface degradation of these boride-based components.
An ultra-thin alumina barrier can be deposited on the components by atomic layer deposition.
A graded coating–substrate interface will enhance adhesion.
A graded interface will minimize thermal mismatch between alumina and the boride substrate.
The graded ALD alumina layer will form a dense, conformal, and adherent interface on the boride substrate.
A dense and intact oxide barrier retards transport through the surface layer.
The alumina layer will physically block and retard diffusion of molten aluminum into the boride substrate.
Alumina is sufficiently chemically inert and thermally stable under the proposed molten-aluminum exposure.
Reducing direct contact and aluminum diffusion will slow the corrosive reactions that degrade the boride component.
Surface oxide formation can improve corrosion resistance of a metallic substrate.
ALD-coated boride components will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than untreated components under identical molten-aluminum exposure.
ALD-coated samples will show lower weight loss than untreated samples.
ALD-coated samples will show shallower aluminum penetration than untreated samples.
The protection is contingent on the alumina layer being defect-free, properly graded, and of an appropriate ultra-thin thickness.
Layer defects or loss of integrity can reduce protection, especially under extreme thermal stress.
The coating should be evaluated at approximately 660°C under repeated thermal cycling and oxidizing/reducing conditions representative of hot-dip aluminum plating.
A controlled comparison of coated and untreated samples can test the predicted protection using weight change, microscopy, and elemental diffusion profiles.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in weight loss, aluminum penetration depth, or microstructural degradation relative to the untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
